To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the combination of phonetic, lexical and prosodic cues improves the affective state prediction, and that the affective lexicon can be used as a complementary feature to improve the affective state recognition.

the phonetic features (degree of articulation and voice quality), the affect lexicon, the expressive prosodic models and the ComParE features are relevant cues for the affective state classification task.

(i) the phonetic and lexical features are more relevant than prosodic features for predicting the affective state of the speaker; (ii) the affect lexicon is more relevant for the Challenge task than the reference lexicon, which is not specific to the task; (iii) the expressive prosodic features are not relevant for the Challenge.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the extraction of linguistic features related to the affective state of mind.
the extraction of linguistic features related to the perception o f emotional valence.
the study of the phonetic, lexical and prosodic cues that can be used in order t o improve the performance of a valence classification task.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the phonetic and prosodic cues are the most relevant for the Challenge task.
the phonetic features, the lexical features and the prosodic features are all useful for the affective state prediction task.
the phonetic and prosodic features have a positive impact on the emotion classification, whereas the lexical ones have a negative impact.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

(i) the degree-of-articula tion and the voice quality are the most relevant phonetic fea tures for the valence classification task; (ii) the lexical cue is relevant but the polarity lexicon is not as accurate as the affect lexicon; and (iii) the expressive prosodic cues are not significant for the valence task.

the combination o f the three linguistic levels (phonetics, lexica l and prosody) is the most efficient approach in the prediction of emotional valence from speech.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the combination of phonetic, lexical an d prosodic features can improve the prediction of the self-assessed emotional state.
the lexical cues are the most promising for the self- assessed affect classification task.
a multi-level analysis of the linguistic cues can be a valuable resource in the design of a self-assessed affect classifier.
